content.problem: A trained dense layer already works, but the task changes. Can we fit the change while leaving the original weights untouched? We will first train a base, then learn and audit a low-rank update.
content.idea: LoRA adds a trainable low-rank correction to a frozen weight map. The base still participates in the forward pass while a smaller set of factors adapts the output. Shape convention and scaling determine how those paths combine.
objectives: Separate the frozen base from trainable adapters
Understand initialization and the first gradient
Verify the changed-condition exercise and explain the limits of this fixture.

sections.title: Separate the frozen path from the low-rank correction
sections.body:
LoRA is useful when a pretrained mapping already contains behavior worth retaining and the new task may need only a limited change. Instead of optimizing every entry of \(W_0\), add a low-rank update. In this fixture, \(W_0\) is \(6\times4\), so rank one uses factors of shapes \(6\times1\) and \(1\times4\), or \(10\) adapter values for \(24\) base values. The base still runs in the forward pass; freezing stops its updates, not its computation.

The recorded adaptation loss goes from \(0.04387\) to \(2.47\times10^{-7}\), consistent with a target deliberately constructed to be rank one. Read the gradient panel next: it explains why training begins even though one factor starts with zero gradient.

check.prompt: If rank changes while alpha stays fixed, can you omit the scaling when merging?
check.answer: No. Merge the exact scaled correction used in forward computation. Otherwise the merged model computes a different function.

sections.title: Before coding: adapt a change, not an entire matrix
sections.body: Think of the source mapping as already useful and the adapter as a constrained correction. The factors first compress an input of width \(d\) into \(r\) coordinates and then expand to output width \(k\). Their product cannot represent a change of rank greater than \(r\), no matter how long it trains. That limit saves trainable parameters when the needed change is low rank, while also predicting which tasks may not fit.

sections.title: Separate the frozen base from trainable adapters
sections.body: For input-by-output weights \(W_0\), the dense branch computes \(xW_0\); the adapter branch computes \(s(xA)B\), where \(s=\alpha/r\). Add the two outputs. Pass only \(A,B\) to the gradient function and retain a copy of \(W_0\). After fitting, compare that copy exactly: it verifies the frozen parameter contract, while the forward diagram shows why the base remains part of every prediction.

sections.title: Understand initialization and the first gradient
sections.body: Initialize \(A\) randomly and \(B\) to zero. Then \(AB=0\), so the starting output matches the base exactly. Because the derivative for \(A\) is multiplied by \(B\), its first gradient is zero; \(B\) can receive a gradient through the nonzero random \(A\). The recorded fixture confirms this asymmetry, and its all-zero control gives zero first gradients for both factors. After \(B\) moves, \(A\) can learn too. Check these gradients before changing the learning rate.

sections.title: Derive the first-step asymmetry
sections.body: Let \(G\) be the gradient at the dense output and \(s=\alpha/r\). Differentiating \(s(xA)B\) gives \(\nabla_A L=sx^TGB^T\) and \(\nabla_B L=s(xA)^TG\). Setting \(B=0\) makes the first expression zero while the second can remain nonzero. Both-zero initialization blocks both. The recorded matrix-calculus check matches JAX at \(\alpha/r=1.5\), so this first-step pattern is a consequence of the parameterization.

sections.title: Use rank to predict a failure before training
sections.body: Rank is a capacity choice, not just a speed dial. A rank-one matrix cannot represent two independent singular directions: for singular values \(3\) and \(1\), its best approximation leaves squared Frobenius error \(1\). In the identity-input exercise, the best rank-one MSE is \(0.25\). More optimization steps cannot remove that representation limit. The main target is itself rank one, so its near-zero loss is expected; compare ranks on a harder held-out target to learn whether the constraint is useful.

sections.title: Count the right kind of savings
sections.body: Count trainable values separately from total memory. Here the base has \(24\) weights and rank one adds \(6\)+\(4\)=\(10\) trainable scalars. The base remains resident, while training also needs adapter gradients, optimizer state, activations, and runtime buffers. The scalar count therefore shows the parameter reduction, not a complete memory or speed measurement. The low-bit frozen-base variant would add quantization and kernel requirements; this exercise does not implement QLoRA.

sections.title: Merge only under an explicit serving contract
sections.body: At inference, the two branches can be combined as \(W_{merged}=W_0+(\alpha/r)AB\) when there is no adapter dropout. The recorded check compares separate and merged outputs on new inputs; it also shows that applying the merge twice changes outputs. Keep the original base and adapter, include scale metadata, and verify after reload before serving. Quantized or packed weights need an explicit conversion contract.

sections.title: Save the adaptation identity
sections.body: Make the adapter artifact identify the function it modifies: base checkpoint hash, target module names, rank, alpha, dtype, and factor arrays. Check adapted-task fit and source-task retention independently. The frozen base values are preserved here, but that alone cannot guarantee the combined model preserves old behavior; the rank-one teacher also does not tell you what rank a real task needs.

sections.title: Make an adapter artifact reproducible
sections.body: Treat reload as part of the serving contract. Store the base identity, tensor orientation and shapes, target layers, rank, alpha, scale rule, dtype, and exact factors. In the fixture, rank two with \(\alpha=3\) means scale \(1.5\); rank one with \(\alpha=1\) would hide a missing scale because it equals one. The recorded fresh-process round trip reproduces predictions at scale \(1.5\), while altered same-shape base values and incorrect rank, alpha, target, or shape metadata are rejected. Keep a source-task metric when assessing behavior after the update.

sections.title: Bind adapter tensors to the exact base and reject shape-compatible substitutes
sections.body: The diagram traces one input through the frozen \(6\times4\) base branch and through trainable \(A\) and \(B\), then scales the adapter output by \(\alpha/r\) before addition. The branches both produce four output features. The arrows show forward dataflow; only adapter factors receive parameter updates. If rank changes while alpha stays fixed, recompute the scale before merging.

content.code:
# Step 1 — 1. Define the frozen-plus-adapter forward pass
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np

def lora_forward(x, base, a, b, alpha=1.0):
    rank = a.shape[1]
    return x @ base + (alpha / rank) * (x @ a @ b)

# Step 2 — 2. Train a base, freeze it and initialize the adapter: This step includes the source-task training.
x = jnp.asarray(np.random.default_rng(4).normal(size=(24, 6)), jnp.float32)
source_w = jnp.arange(24, dtype=jnp.float32).reshape(6, 4) / 40
base = jnp.zeros_like(source_w)
base_step = jax.jit(jax.grad(lambda w: jnp.mean((x @ w - x @ source_w) ** 2)))
for _ in range(150):
    base = base - 0.15 * base_step(base)
assert float(jnp.mean((x @ base - x @ source_w) ** 2)) < 1e-4
# Transfer the device result to the host for an independent NumPy comparison.
frozen = np.asarray(base).copy()
u = jnp.array([[0.2], [-0.3], [0.1], [0.2], [-0.1], [0.4]])
v = jnp.array([[0.5, -0.2, 0.3, 0.1]])
target = x @ (base + u @ v)
a = jax.random.normal(jax.random.key(4), (6, 1)) * 0.1
b = jnp.zeros((1, 4))
params = (a, b)
loss = lambda ab: jnp.mean((lora_forward(x, base, *ab, alpha=1.0) - target) ** 2)
step = jax.jit(jax.value_and_grad(loss))
history = []
initial_grads = step(params)[1]
np.testing.assert_array_equal(initial_grads[0], np.zeros((6, 1)))
assert np.linalg.norm(initial_grads[1]) > 0

# Step 3 — 3. Adapt and verify the serving merge: The reference target has rank one by construction.
for _ in range(250):
    value, g = step(params)
    history.append(float(value))
    params = jax.tree.map(lambda a, b: a - 0.4 * b, params, g)

a, b = params
assert history[-1] < history[0] * 0.02
np.testing.assert_array_equal(base, frozen)
merged = base + a @ b
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    lora_forward(x, base, a, b), x @ merged, rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-6
)
print(
    'LoRA initial/final:',
    history[0],
    history[-1],
    '; trainable:',
    a.size + b.size,
    'base:',
    base.size,
)
content.output: The trained base stays unchanged; 10 adapter scalars fit the rank-one change and merge equivalently.

experiments.title: Show why two zero factors cannot start learning
experiments.prediction: If both factors start at zero, can this first-order update move either one?
experiments.code:
# Experiment — Show why two zero factors cannot start learning: Each factor’s derivative contains the other factor.
zero = (jnp.zeros_like(a), jnp.zeros_like(b))
zero_grad = jax.grad(loss)(zero)
assert all(
    np.array_equal(np.asarray(g), np.zeros(g.shape)) for g in zero_grad
)
print('Both zero factors produce zero first gradients.')
experiments.output: Both factor gradients are exactly zero.
experiments.explanation: Each factor’s derivative contains the other factor. Randomizing one and zeroing the other preserves the initial base output without blocking the whole update.

experiments.title: Check both factor gradients with matrix calculus
experiments.prediction: At nonzero factors, will the two matrix-gradient formulas agree with autodiff including nonunit alpha?
experiments.code:
# Experiment — Check both factor gradients with matrix calculus
rng = np.random.default_rng(14)
a_probe = jnp.asarray(rng.normal(size=(6, 2)) * 0.1, jnp.float32)
b_probe = jnp.asarray(rng.normal(size=(2, 4)) * 0.1, jnp.float32)
scale = 3.0 / 2
output_gradient = (
    2 * (lora_forward(x, base, a_probe, b_probe, 3.0) - target) / target.size
)
expected_a = scale * x.T @ output_gradient @ b_probe.T
expected_b = scale * a_probe.T @ x.T @ output_gradient
actual_a, actual_b = jax.grad(
    lambda aa, bb: jnp.mean(
        (lora_forward(x, base, aa, bb, 3.0) - target) ** 2
    ),
    argnums=(0, 1),
)(a_probe, b_probe)
np.testing.assert_allclose(actual_a, expected_a, atol=1e-6)
np.testing.assert_allclose(actual_b, expected_b, atol=1e-6)
print('Both LoRA factor gradients match the matrix-calculus oracle at alpha/r = 1.5.')
experiments.output: Both factor derivatives match the independent output-gradient calculation.
experiments.explanation: Nonzero factors exercise both gradient paths, while nonunit scaling catches a factor missing from the derivative. The separate all-zero experiment demonstrates the initialization failure.

practice.title: Test nonunit scaling and an impossible rank-one target
practice.prompt: Check merge equivalence at rank two with alpha three. Then use identity inputs and a diagonal target with singular values three and one to calculate the best rank-one residual.
practice.hint: Use an independent singular-value decomposition for the rank bound, and divide alpha by rank in both serving paths.
practice.solution:
# Test nonunit scaling and an impossible rank-one target (Challenge)
rng = np.random.default_rng(8)
a2 = jnp.asarray(rng.normal(size=(6, 2)), jnp.float32)
b2 = jnp.asarray(rng.normal(size=(2, 4)), jnp.float32)
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    lora_forward(x, base, a2, b2, alpha=3.0),
    x @ (base + 1.5 * a2 @ b2),
    rtol=1e-5,
    atol=2e-6,
)
target_update = np.diag([3.0, 1.0])
u_s, s_s, v_s = np.linalg.svd(target_update)
rank_one = (u_s[:, :1] * s_s[:1]) @ v_s[:1]
np.testing.assert_allclose(np.sum((target_update - rank_one) ** 2), 1.0)
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    np.mean((np.eye(2) @ target_update - np.eye(2) @ rank_one) ** 2), 0.25
)
print('Nonunit scaling passes; best rank-one identity-input MSE is 0.25.')
practice.explanation: The residual predicts a capacity limit independently of an optimizer. The nonunit-alpha case catches a scaling bug that the main rank-one demonstration would miss.

practice.title: Enforce base identity in a fresh-process adapter reload
practice.prompt: Use the actual trained rank-two alpha-three factors from a bounded teaching fit on the frozen fitted base, then extend the save exercise so it writes a checkpoint hash and manifest, then loads the base and adapter in a separate Python process. Use rank two and alpha three. Verify merged/unmerged predictions on changed inputs. Reject a different same-shape base and altered rank, alpha, target-module, or tensor-shape metadata before inference.
practice.hint: Hash the exact serialized base file bytes. Validate manifest fields and array shapes/dtypes before calculating the adapter branch. Do not compare only parameter shapes.
practice.solution:
# Fresh-process adapter bundle round trip with base identity and negative controls.
import hashlib, json, os, subprocess, sys, tempfile
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(815)
base2 = np.asarray(base, dtype=np.float32).copy()
base_before_adapter_fit = base2.copy()
alpha, rank = 3.0, 2
scale = alpha / rank
# A bounded rank-two teaching target; fit the factors before serializing them.
u2 = jnp.asarray([[0.2, -0.1], [-0.3, 0.1], [0.1, 0.2], [0.2, -0.2], [-0.1, 0.1], [0.4, 0.2]], jnp.float32)
v2 = jnp.asarray([[0.5, -0.2, 0.3, 0.1], [-0.1, 0.4, 0.2, -0.3]], jnp.float32)
target2 = x @ (jnp.asarray(base2) + scale * u2 @ v2)
a2 = jax.random.normal(jax.random.key(815), (6, rank)) * 0.1
b2 = jnp.zeros((rank, 4), jnp.float32)
fit2 = jax.jit(jax.value_and_grad(lambda aa, bb: jnp.mean(
    (lora_forward(x, jnp.asarray(base2), aa, bb, alpha) - target2) ** 2
), argnums=(0, 1)))
fit_history = []
for _ in range(300):
    fit_loss, (grad_a, grad_b) = fit2(a2, b2)
    fit_history.append(float(fit_loss))
    a2 = a2 - 0.2 * grad_a
    b2 = b2 - 0.2 * grad_b
assert fit_history[-1] < fit_history[0] * 1e-3
np.testing.assert_array_equal(base2, base_before_adapter_fit)
a2 = np.asarray(a2, dtype=np.float32)
b2 = np.asarray(b2, dtype=np.float32)
changed_x = rng.normal(size=(5, 6)).astype(np.float32)
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    root = Path(tmp)
    np.save(root / "base.npy", base2, allow_pickle=False)
    np.savez(root / "adapter.npz", A=a2, B=b2)
    with np.load(root / "adapter.npz", allow_pickle=False) as trained_bundle:
        np.testing.assert_array_equal(trained_bundle["A"], a2)
        np.testing.assert_array_equal(trained_bundle["B"], b2)
    base_hash = hashlib.sha256((root / "base.npy").read_bytes()).hexdigest()
    manifest = {
        "schema": 1, "base_sha256": base_hash,
        "target_modules": ["decoder.block.0.proj"],
        "base_shape": list(base2.shape), "base_dtype": str(base2.dtype),
        "rank": rank, "alpha": alpha, "scaling": "alpha_over_rank",
        "A_shape": list(a2.shape), "B_shape": list(b2.shape),
        "A_dtype": str(a2.dtype), "B_dtype": str(b2.dtype),
    }
    (root / "manifest.json").write_text(json.dumps(manifest, sort_keys=True))
    # New interpreter reloads all three artifacts from disk and validates before activation.
    child = r"""import hashlib,json,sys
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
root=Path(sys.argv[1]); m=json.loads((root/'manifest.json').read_text())
base_path=Path(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv)>2 else root/'base.npy'
base_bytes=base_path.read_bytes()
if hashlib.sha256(base_bytes).hexdigest()!=m['base_sha256']: raise ValueError('base checkpoint identity mismatch')
base=np.load(base_path,allow_pickle=False)
with np.load(root/'adapter.npz',allow_pickle=False) as z: A=z['A']; B=z['B']
if list(base.shape)!=m['base_shape'] or str(base.dtype)!=m['base_dtype']: raise ValueError('base shape/dtype mismatch')
if list(A.shape)!=m['A_shape'] or list(B.shape)!=m['B_shape'] or str(A.dtype)!=m['A_dtype'] or str(B.dtype)!=m['B_dtype']: raise ValueError('adapter tensor metadata mismatch')
if m['rank']!=A.shape[1] or B.shape[0]!=m['rank'] or m['scaling']!='alpha_over_rank' or m['alpha']!=3.0: raise ValueError('rank/scaling metadata mismatch')
if m['target_modules']!=['decoder.block.0.proj']: raise ValueError('target module mismatch')
x=np.load(root/'inputs.npy',allow_pickle=False); scale=m['alpha']/m['rank']
separate=x@base+scale*(x@A@B); merged=x@(base+scale*A@B)
np.testing.assert_allclose(separate,merged,rtol=1e-6,atol=1e-6)
np.save(root/'child-predictions.npy',separate,allow_pickle=False)
print('fresh-process validated',m['base_sha256'],float(np.max(np.abs(separate-merged))))"""
    np.save(root / "inputs.npy", changed_x, allow_pickle=False)
    subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", child, str(root)], check=True, capture_output=True, text=True)
    child_predictions = np.load(root / "child-predictions.npy", allow_pickle=False)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(child_predictions, changed_x @ base2 + 1.5 * (changed_x @ a2 @ b2), rtol=1e-6, atol=1e-6)
    # Shape-compatible wrong base must fail on the base digest before activation.
    wrong = base2.copy(); wrong[0, 0] += 0.25
    np.save(root / "wrong-base.npy", wrong, allow_pickle=False)
    result = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", child, str(root), str(root / "wrong-base.npy")], capture_output=True, text=True)
    assert result.returncode != 0 and "base checkpoint identity mismatch" in result.stderr
    # Each incompatible metadata edit must fail before predictions are activated.
    negatives = [
        ("rank", 1, "rank/scaling metadata mismatch"),
        ("alpha", 4.0, "rank/scaling metadata mismatch"),
        ("target_modules", ["decoder.block.1.proj"], "target module mismatch"),
        ("A_shape", [6, 1], "adapter tensor metadata mismatch"),
    ]
    for field, value, message in negatives:
        bad = dict(manifest, **{field: value})
        (root / "manifest.json").write_text(json.dumps(bad, sort_keys=True))
        result = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", child, str(root)], capture_output=True, text=True)
        assert result.returncode != 0 and message in result.stderr, (field, result.stderr)
print("rank-two alpha/r=1.5 teaching-fit loss:", fit_history[0], fit_history[-1])
print("Fresh-process trained-factor round trip passed at alpha/r=1.5; wrong same-shape base and altered rank, alpha, target, and shape metadata were rejected.")
practice.explanation: The new rank-two factors are fitted on the existing frozen base before save, and the child interpreter reloads those exact trained factor bytes. The child interpreter reads only serialized files and validates the base digest before multiplying. The rank-two, alpha-three case exercises nonunit scaling. New inputs check the serving merge algebra after reload. The wrong base has exactly the same dimensions and dtype; the hash is what distinguishes its identity. Manifest changes must be validated against tensor geometry and the declared scale before an adapter can be applied.

content.question: Does LoRA require updating the base weights during adapter training?
options: No. The base is frozen; the selected adapter parameters receive updates.
Yes, because initializing factor \(B=0\) blocks all gradients until the base matrix moves.
No, and freezing the base weights guarantees that adapted outputs cannot forget the source task.
content.explanation: LoRA freezes the base parameters while optimizing the named adapter parameters. Verify parameter ownership and actual before/after deltas. Frozen base storage does not imply unchanged behavior or retained capability.
content.diagnosis: If neither factor moves, inspect initialization. If merged predictions drift, check factor orientation, rank scaling, dropout, base identity and accidental repeated merges.

The second panel shows initial factor-gradient norms: A is zero because B starts at zero, while B is nonzero and can start learning. The both-zero control confirms that zeroing both factors would block the first update. import jax

def lora_forward(x, base, a, b, alpha=1.0):

x = jnp.asarray(np.random.default_rng(4).normal(size=(24, 6)), jnp.float32)

for _ in range(150):
    base = base - 0.15 * base_step(base)
assert float(jnp.mean((x @ base - x @ source_w) ** 2)) < 1e-4
# Transfer the device result to the host for an independent NumPy comparison.
frozen = np.asarray(base).copy()
u = jnp.array([[0.2], [-0.3], [0.1], [0.2], [-0.1], [0.4]])
v = jnp.array([[0.5, -0.2, 0.3, 0.1]])

np.testing.assert_array_equal(initial_grads[0], np.zeros((6, 1)))

for _ in range(250):
    value, g = step(params)
    history.append(float(value))
    params = jax.tree.map(lambda a, b: a - 0.4 * b, params, g)

a, b = params
assert history[-1] < history[0] * 0.02
np.testing.assert_array_equal(base, frozen)
merged = base + a @ b
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    lora_forward(x, base, a, b), x @ merged, rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-6
)
print(
    'LoRA initial/final:',
    history[0],
    history[-1],
    '; trainable:',
    a.size + b.size,
    'base:',

Adapters can alter behavior even when the base weights are frozen. Test retention and task quality rather than inferring them from frozen storage.
